title: One line
hookLine: learn one short refrain and sing only that

lines: THE LINE THAT LIVES IN YOUR HEAD.
cards: A single line of a song can live in a head for years. A lullaby a grandmother sang, a hymn from school, the chorus of a song from a hard summer. The verses are long gone, or were never learned.
But that one line comes back, uninvited, in the shower, on a long drive, in a hospital waiting room. It has been doing quiet work all along. Nobody needed the whole song.
The line was enough. Today, one line: a single short refrain from the Guru's hymns, learned well enough to carry around.

teach.b: Here's a gentle rule some kirtan teachers give beginners: don't try to learn a whole shabad. Learn one line, and sing only that, again and again, until it's yours. Which line?
A few good places to look. The rahao line, from day one hundred seven, the heart of a hymn and already built to be repeated.

teach.h: THE RAHAO, OR IK ONKAR, SATNAM.
teach.b: The opening of the Mool Mantar you met on days four and five: Ik Onkar, Satnam. Or a short line from any shabad that caught you this week. Why is one line enough?
Because of what the Gurus say a single teaching can do.

teach.h: GEMS, IF YOU HEAR EVEN ONE TEACHING.
teach.b: In the Japji, Guru Nanak says, in paraphrase, that within the mind are gems, jewels and rubies, if you listen to even one teaching of the Guru. Even one. The Gurus weren't asking people to memorize a library.
They trusted that one true line, really taken in, can open the rest.

And a sung line goes deeper than a read one. You've learned it with your breath, your ear and your voice, not just your eyes. That's why it comes back uninvited, at the right moments, the way that old song does.
Some Sikhs talk about a line of gurbani, a tuk, staying with them through a hard year, or rising up at a funeral, or at a wedding. Nobody planned it. The line had been waiting.

how: Many Sikhs carry a favorite line of gurbani, a tuk, that they sing or repeat through the day, and kirtan teachers often start beginners with a single refrain.

games.why: one line, sung until it's yours. Guru Nanak says even one teaching, truly heard, holds gems.

practice: Choose one short line; if you're not sure, take Ik Onkar, Satnam, and say it once, slowly, to be sure of the sounds.

Then sing it softly on two or three notes, or on yesterday's Waheguru tune, again and again, letting it get easier each time. Don't reach for a second line; stay with this one until it's as familiar as your own name.
